The Use of DSC and Independent Oxygen Analyses to Correlate the β Transus Temperature in CP-Ti Grade 2 Materials Processed via Different Techniques
recent_works.abstract: Abstract Detecting oxygen content in commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti) is essential, especially in additive manufacturing processes where contamination is problematic. Traditional analyses are expensive and require significant amounts of material. In titanium, oxygen content corresponds to increasing β transus temperatures. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) was used on titanium materials to determine β transus temperatures, which were confirmed by independent oxygen analyses, and used in CALPHAD modeling. Analysis suggested DSC could be a less expensive method of determining oxygen content in CP-Ti.

recent_works.title: Angle-resolved polarized Raman spectroscopy study of phosphorene nanoribbons
recent_works.abstract: We present a systematic angle-resolved polarized Raman spectroscopy (ARPRS) study of black phosphorus (BP) nanostructures formed via electrochemical sodium- and lithium-ion intercalation. Sodium intercalation leads to bundles of densely packed, highly uniform phosphorene nanoribbons (PNRs) separated by parallel amorphous channels, whereas lithium intercalation results in shorter, irregular nanoribbon-like segments with lower aspect ratios. In both cases, six additional Raman peaks (P1–P6) appear alongside the three primary Raman-active modes of BP (A1g, B2g, and A2g). These peaks are attributed to the amorphous regions, as confirmed by their isotropic angular dependence in ARPRS measurements. The three BP modes show pronounced angular variations that differ significantly between the two intercalated samples. In sodium-intercalated BP, A1g and A2g modes retain a dumbbell-like angular dependence under parallel polarization with enhanced anisotropy and reduced symmetry under crossed polarization. recent_works.title: GAN-Generated Face Detection with Advanced Deep Neural Network Architectures and Pre-Processing Techniques
recent_works.abstract: The incredible hyper-realism that Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have been able to produce in recent years-including photographs of human faces-makes it very difficult to distinguish genuine photos from fakes. In order to identify GAN-generated faces, this research suggests a particular architecture for deep neural networks (DNNs). For each category, the DNN model learns complex features and patterns from a large dataset that includes both actual and GAN-generated face photos. The model's generalizability and robustness are improved by using advanced preprocessing methods, such as data normalization and augmentation. In order to accomplish the classification job, the design makes use of fully connected layers after convolutional layers have extracted high-level information. The proposed DNN outperforms conventional image analysis techniques in experiments that compare GAN-generated images to genuine faces, demonstrating great accuracy in face detection. In addition to adding to the expanding corpus of literature in digital picture forensics, this study highlights the need for trustworthy detection methods to prevent the possible abuse of GAN-generated information.
